subsubtopic: ALLOTED DAY, S.O. 82-ECONOMIC FUTURE OF REGION OF GREATER MONTREAL
speechtext:
That this House condemns the Government for its failure to act in matters of interest to the region of Greater Montreal, including the space agency, the development of the Vieux-Port, the planning and development of Montreal Harbour, the Soligaz project, the shipyards and the economic renewal of East Montreal as well as the economic deterioration of the southwestern part of the region.
He said: Mr. Speaker, I think it is important to recall why today, we in the Liberal Party move this motion to condemn a Government that has been in power for three and half years, a motion that concerns matters of interest to Montreal, the main urban centre of Quebec and one of the major urban centres in this country. Why has the number of issues outstanding increased to the point that today, we moved a motion condemning the Government? We must remember that after the election in 1984, following the many promises made by this Government to the people of Montreal, the municipal authorities and Quebecers as a whole, that in 1985, despite strong representation consisting of fifty-six or fifty-seven Members, including eight Conservative Members on Montreal Island, the business community started to complain.
The business community was disappointed because they found there was no one, no Members with enough clout to defend the interests of the Montreal community. Right away, both employers and employees, sensing they had no one to defend their interests, turned to the Opposition. This started in Montreal East. When representatives of employees at Bombardier, Vickers and Gulf, where shutdowns were a very real threat, realized they were not getting satisfactory answers from Conservative Members, they went to see the Opposition Members in the Liberal Party, in their search for ways to make themselves heard, to defend their cause, save jobs and save the economy.
Right away, on November 15, we in the Liberal Party set up a survival committee. Considering the gravity of the situation in Montreal East at the time with eight companies that were about to close down, which would result in the direct loss of 2,400 jobs and the loss of 5,000 jobs indirectly at the request of my colleagues from Papineau and Laval-des-Rapides (Messrs. Ouellet and Garneau), I set up this survival committee for Montreal East, including as members all socio-economic and even political intervenors representing government at the provincial and municipal levels, in order to put pressure on the federal Government so that it would act and respond to expectations and needs and deal with the emergency situation facing these people who were about to lose their jobs.
Under this kind of pressure exerted as much by the Montreal business community as by federal, provincial and municipal political interests, not to mention the very strong Montreal East concertation group, at long last the Conservative Government-and the Prime Minister, of course-realizes it is in a very difficult situation and that nobody is adequately prepared to defend the interests of the Montreal region. And so, on December 5, the Prime Minister announces his decision to strike a Cabinet committee whose members will study and prepare the economic revival of Greater Montreal. Listen now, make a note of the people who were selected for the Cabinet committee, and I quote the article published in Le Devoir after the Prime Minister's Office issued its release:
The President of the Treasury Board (Mr. de Cotret), the then Minister of Transport (Mr. Mazankowski), the then Secretary of State (Mr. Bouchard), the Minister of State (Small Businesses) (Mr. Bissonnette), and two Ministers from the Island of Montreal, Mrs. Suzanne Blais-Grenier, then Minister of State (Transport), and Mr. Robert Layton, Minister of State (Mines).
If you check the list you will see that four of them went their separate way, four of them simply took off: Mr. Layton, the former Minister of State (Mines), as he is referred to in the release, was downgraded: the Hon. Member for Rosemont (Mrs. Blais-Grenier) who was Minister of State (Transport) was also given a pink slip; and of course we all know the whereabouts of the ex-Minister of State (Small Businesses) (Mr. Bissonette). Consider all these people and you have a fair idea of the consequences.
The day after, the present Minister of Regional Industrial Expansion (Mr. de Cotret) lifts the wrap off the new Consultative Committee on the Development of the Montreal Region

headed by Mr. Picard. The committee is made up of people from different fields-management, labour unions, and spokesmen for the municipal, provincial and federal administrations-who will examine the file, because the Conservatives have just come down to earth and they simply do not know what Montreal needs. Bear in mind the many generous promises which had been made by the Prime Minister; he had said Montreal would become the international city. All at once he realizes what he had promised-he did not really know what he had been saying-so he comes up with a Cabinet committee and the Picard Committee.
To put matters in their proper context, I would like to remind the House of the issues which were urgent at the time and of the reasons why the Picard Committee was created. In addition, the Pichette Committee was created and examined many problems in Montreal East. All this occurred in 1985.
Let us look at all the problems one by one. In Montreal East, in November 1985, Bombardier was threatening to close down and we also witnessed the closing of Canadian Steel Wheel, Canadian Steel Foundries, Vickers, Daoust-Lalonde, La Parisette, SKD and the Gulf refinery. We also remember all that happened at the time, including the divisions within the Conservative Party, including a resignation, over the Gulf refinery issue. Each time, the Survival Committee organized meetings. People came to demonstrate on Parliament Hill. Representatives of Bombardier, Vickers, and Gulf employees met, in Ottawa and in Montreal, either the Minister whom I referred to earlier, who was responsible for the Ministerial Committee, or the then Secretary of State, who is now Minister of Employment and Immigration (Mr. Bouchard), and each time, all they got were vague replies, but no concrete action from the federal Government.
Now, after three years of a hard-fought battle, the federal Government has decided to allow Ultramar to purchase the Gulf refinery and to close it down, even though Gaz Metropo-litain and other companies were willing to purchase the refinery and to keep it in operation. Let us be honest: I already know what the Tory Members are going to say: when you were the Government, there were two other refineries which had to close down and how come the Hon. Member for Montreal- Sainte-Marie ... There is a difference.
In the case of the SKD Company ... I am not blaming the Tory Members for a company that moved its head office or plant from one province to another because for the time being we have no way to stop that. If the Gulf Company had said: Look, I am closing my refinery here because I would rather operate the one in Ontario, we would have said, as we all disagreed at the time... and I remember that the Hon. Member for Mercier at the time was against the closing down of refineries, but there is no legislation to prevent that now, and it is the same in Quebec, there is no mechanism to stop a corporation from closing its facilities in Montreal and transferring them to Quebec city to ...
Often, in the textile industry, businesses close their plant in Montreal to move to the Eastern Townships. There is no legislation to prevent them from doing so, for it is a matter of internal economy. But then, in the case of the Gulf refinery it is different: first of all, the Federal Government asked Petro-Canada to buy everything, except in Quebec. That is serious. Moreover, there was a second opportunity to prevent the closing of the Gulf refinery, which did not exist in other areas before whereby, Ultramar being a foreign company-and the Government had changed what was called the FIRA and we now had Investment Canada-Ultramar, in fact is a British company which had to obtain the autorization of the Federal Government, the Cabinet, the Prime Minister, to complete this transaction. We know at that time, that other corporations were willing to buy ... Therefore, if the Canadian Government had truly wanted to save the Gulf refinery, not only because of the loss of 450 jobs, but also for the refining capacity and the protection of consumers, they would have said no to this transaction and called on other prospective buyers or they could even have asked Petro-Canada to purchase and improve its refining system in Montreal East. No, we remember what happened. It was during the Christmas and New Year's recess.
The former Minister of Regional Industrial Expansion, Mr. Stevens, came to Montreal, and at the same time he announced what I must admit were good news about Petromont, which you had reason to welcome, Mr. Speaker, he announced the demise of the Gulf refinery in Montreal East without any Cabinet representatives from Quebec being present. The Conservative Government thought nothing would happen since it caught Montrealers and Quebecers by surprise. No way! A coalition to save the Gulf refinery was organized in no time. Even though that occurred during the holiday season, activities were co-ordinated and today, thanks not to the Conservative Government but to the Government of Quebec, the facilities of the Gulf refinery remain in place, 250 workers have returned to their jobs and there is hope for the Montreal East refinery and the petro-chemical industry.
But in the meantime, unfortunately, a Minister resigned, whether that was the reason or she was on the verge of dismissal before that, but anyway a Minister said she was resigning because her government made an uninformed decision. A Conservative Member, the Member for Terrebonne (Mr. Toupin), switched parties on that issue. And internal conflicts divided Conservative members on the issue of the Gulf refinery.
The result, today: I owe thanks to the Minister of Energy of Quebec, John Caccia, and congratulations to people such as Serge Baril, Luc Chouinard and M. Tremblay who never stopped fighting to save those workers' jobs.
What about other corporations? Namely, Bombardier and Vickers. Those people in Bombardier... further to our initiatives at the consultation table, we succeeded in getting contracts for New York subway trains-this saved jobs. And
March 18, 1988

recently, again under pressure, we got a contract for 50 locomotives.
As a result, people in Montreal East today can be proud, and they deserve to be congratulated for the way they acted together, the way they closed ranks by rising above political partisanship-,both city concillors and MLA's and labour leaders, because at that consultation table, on that survival committee there were people from the CNMTU, the QFL and people in so-called shop unions that are usually competing among themselves. But on that survival committee, people showed solidarity.
Today, there is reason to rejoice after 25 months of work, the efforts of five Liberal MPs who acted on that matter, in a daily, constant way, pushing on Ministers in this House. There were my colleagues for Laval-des-Rapides (Mr. Garneau), for Saint-Leonard-Anjou (Mr. Gagliano), for Saint-Jacques (Mr. Guilbault) and for Saint-Denis (Mr. Prud'homme), as well as my colleagues for Papineau (Mr. Ouellet) and Shefford (Mr. Lapierre) who lent us a hand and were regularly urging the Government, following up the matter, asking questions, doing research with Government departments.
With that stocktaking in Montreal East now, I say: Well done to the City of Montreal which announced $90 million over five years to modernize and develop the industrial base. I say: Well done to the Quebec Government which announced $105 million over three years, a large percentage of which is going not only toward corporate modernization but also toward the so-called workers' "employability".
The important thing to come out of Pichette Committee studies is that in Montreal East there were 22,000 unemployed, 12,000 welfare recipients. And if tomorrow a business were to be set up there, there is no certainty those people would get the jobs. Moreover, if circumstances changed the nature of a business so that it could no longer operate, there is no certainty that its employees could find jobs in another sector.
The Quebec Government provided financial support for manpower training and re-training programs, as employability of the workers is very important for Montreal East. As usual, we then were disappointed by the announcement of the federal Government. The sad thing is that, although they may try to fool the public, it just does not work.
The Minister of Regional Industrial Expansion went to Montreal and met with the people involved to try to make them believe that he was announcing a subsidy of $210 million. However, it immediately became obvious that there was only $35 million in new money and that the rest would be spent over a five-year period.
It does no good to try to fool the people. The Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) tried it with our senior citizens, but the Members opposite should now stop using this method since they have been found out.

Naturally, the Minister and the Conservative Members who attended the meeting got booed, because people expected more from the federal Government than a few crumbs and a measly $35 million. The Government and the Conservative Members from the Montreal region knew quite well that what was needed was the early retirement program.
This is what was needed in view of the fact the workers who demonstrated had been abandoned because of the lack of a purchasing policy for railway transport and the maritime industry.
I see that the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson) is here. All this certainly happened because he had negotiated with the American Governement his famous so-called free trade agreement. The people of Montreal East are already footing the bill because there is no truly effective policy to ensure the survival of the industries. The people from Bombardier, Canadian Steel Wheel, Canadian La Forge are precisely those who demonstrated.
The result: last weekend, there was an article in La Presse entitled: "Les plaies majeures qui affectent Vest de Montreal" (The major ills plaguing Montreal East). In the end, Mr. Laurent Picard who was appointed to make a study, said the Conservative Government has written off not only Montreal East, but the whole city. The situation is very serious. I only have two minutes left, Mr. Speaker. I have all those other issues to deal with.
The shipyards: there again, promises from the Conservative Government, promises from the Minister responsible for the Quebec region to Minister Johnson. In exchange for deals with the shipyards, the Government promises to divide the frigates contract. More empty promises. The Government was fooled. Even the Hon. Member for Levis (Mr. Fontaine) was quoted in a newspaper article as having said: "Not sharing the contract is unthinkable." The result is that we have been fooled on the frigates matter.
The Soligaz project is another one, which the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Mr. Masse) is holding up, and the Government of Quebec, the people from the East and the industry are waiting to hear about.
There is another sector in Montreal East... also the southwest. There are shutdowns there also, Mr. Speaker. Five businesses closed down, 2,000 jobs are lost. People are waiting for replies to their request of only $130,000 for a study on the issues concerning the southwest area of Montreal.
In the port of Montreal also there is plenty of work to do, and space is lacking. That is also due to the Government's delay or inaction.
Another promise: The Government and the Prime Minister promised a real International Banking Centre that was going to be a revolution. All we have is a night deposit system to accommodate the person who just came from Mexico and spends the night in a Montreal hotel. Another masquerade!

Let us talk now about the Old Port of Montreal. The Liberal Government had acted on this issue. All the other cities in Quebec, in Canada, received money. We want $130 million. The delays in these matters are again due to the incompetence and inaction of the Minister of Regional Industrial Expansion (Mr. de Cotret). We want $130 million, Mr. Speaker, and once again we get nothing.
The scandal on the space agency is out of this world! It is worse than anything, ever. First, ministers are contradicting one another. The Minister of Regional Industrial Expansion was contradicted by his Prime Minister, and you can see clearly in the newspapers reports, Mr. Speaker. I am running out of time. I could go on and on all afternoon, but my colleagues the Hon. Members for Laval-des-Rapides (Mr. Garneau) and for Saint-Denis (Mr. Prud'homme) will take over.
Michel Vastel has clearly shown in his article that this Government has totally abandoned Montreal, because of the low calibre of those who represent that area in the Conservative caucus and in Cabinet. He calls them lackeys. Mayor Dore is furious, Mr. Macdonald, the Minister, says he is fed up with those people who are wasting his time.
Mr. Speaker, where are we today after three years-and 1 see that my time is up-three Hon. Members, three ministers, have been thrown out of the ministerial committee, chaired by the minister of Regional Industrial Expansion, for a variety of reasons-there is nothing left there, Mr. Speaker. Nothing is being done for Montreal. I know that the minister will be giving me numbers, statistics and the like. The jobs created were not of his doing. He is going to come and tell us stories ("tataouinage"). We know all about storytellers! Once again, he is going to pull the wool over our eyes. We have seen it before. People are tired of being taken for a ride, Mr. Speaker.
The best thing that the minister responsible for the Greater Montreal area could announce today is his resignation, considering how he has failed. The Government deserves to be blamed, but the minister responsible for the Montreal area, the minister of Regional Industrial Expansion, should resign on account of his failure over the past three years.
Mir. Langdon: Mr. Speaker, I am interested in the speech made by the Hon. Member. He has made many criticisms but we also want to criticize certains points raised in his motion. I would like to put to him the following question: Had the Hon. Member been able to develop a strategy for Montreal East and for the economy of the south-western area, what would he have done? He referred at length to closures. He also dealt at length with the lack of government policy, but what is the policy of the Liberal party for Montreal East.

Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to answer the question. With respect to Montreal East, as a policy, contrary to the Tories, we did not try to mislead the people. And our leader, the Leader of the Official Opposition (Mr. Turner) met
the citizens of Montreal East, as well as representatives of industries and unions who are not necessarily Liberals. He was not booed, contrary to the Minister when he met those people, and the commitment of the Liberal Party to Montreal East is quite clear. It was first a commitment to inject $50 million of new money, with no tricks such as those played by the Minister. What is more important, the Leader of the Opposition announced what we call the Older Citizens' adjustment Program or what is currently known as pre-retirement.
However a still more important arrangement... The Hon. Member gives me an opportunity to say that during the next weekend, we will hold a symposium and I think that the Liberal members of Montreal East have shown that we could sit down with the people involved and find the necessary funds. This is what we did. We worked in co-operation with civic and provincial authorities. We should not forget that those people have different allegiances. With an elected Liberal Government, our caucus would have a very strong group of Liberal Members representing Montreal East. As a matter of fact, we are considering a resolution calling on a Liberal caucus to meet every month to examine the situation in Montreal East, and once a year, to meet with all social and economic interests, to follow up on that situation and engage in some action. But the problem with regional development policies is that they are not applicable to large urban centers. And that is why we would want some mechanism to have a whole range of economic regional development programs made available to large as well as smaller centers in case of a disaster such as the one that occured in Montreal East.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the subject today is Montreal and I must say I was somewhat surprised by the remarks of the Hon.

March 18, 1988
Supply
Member for Montreal-Sainte-Marie (Mr. Malepart) on this Opposition day, particularly since this Government has done a lot more for Montreal than the previous administration ever did.
For starters, just what is Montreal? Montreal is more than a city. Montreal is more that a physical site. Montreal is a major geographic area. Montreal is an economic motor. Montreal is a cultural motor. Montreal is a place which is vital to Quebec and to the country as a whole. Montreal is an international, financial, high tech city where culture, the arts, tourism play an important part, a city where transportation not only played a significant role, but was at the very origin of its settlement. It is a manufacturing city, a design city. Although Greater Montreal is inhabited by three million people, it is a city which has retained the values of its roots, a city where the residents can enjoy a quality of life rarely found elsewhere in the world, a city where people talk to one another, communicate, converse honestly. It is a city which has suffered great hardships under the previous Government and I will go back to that later.
First of all, I should like to deal with Montreal as a whole. First, our accomplishments: the Hon. Member for Montreal- Sainte-Marie clearly indicated that I was going to quote statistics, and I would not want to disappoint him. Here are some statistics: in Montreal, the number of jobs increased by 114,000 between 1984 and 1987. By contrast, when we refer to the years 1980-1984, while the party of my honourable friend was in power, a net loss of 4,000 jobs was registered. The House will remember that the distinguished Member for Montreal-Sainte-Marie was a backbencher at the time. You would think that our friend was concerned then with the poor performance of his Government and that he was shouting angrily as he is doing now. Quite the contrary! During the three years from 1980 to 1983, while this economic and cultural heart of Quebec was experiencing such a significant slowing down, the Hon. Member for Montreal-Sainte-Marie found the courage to deal with issues affecting Montreal's economy on three occasions only. Without being a mathematician, I can say that it was on an average of once a year. On the other hand, the remarks he was making were not likely to shake the very foundations of the House. But let us say no more!
Has the Government allowed the situation to deteriorate over the past few months? The answer is no! How could he explain the creation of 50,000 new jobs in Montreal over the past 12 months? Fet us take my department for example. Through its various programs, it has granted the Montreal region as a whole a total of nearly $533 million in financial assistance between September 1984 and January 1988. It is estimated that these projects will involve investments of over $2 billion and will directly help to create 19,000 jobs. That is what my Department has done in Montreal East.
Since September 1984, DRIE, through its programs and subsidiary agreements, has injected $39 million in the following federal ridings: Montreal-Sainte-Marie, surprising
as that may seem, and Gamelin, Hochelaga-Maisonneuve, Montreal-Mercier, Rosemont and Saint-Leonard-Anjou.
Mr. Speaker, as you know, despite the sporadic whining of the Opposition, things are really moving in Montreal. Projects are mushrooming.
Looking at my notes, I see that the federal Government helped to set up the departmental committee on the development of the region of Montreal, as well as the advisory committee on the development of the same region, and that many experts from my department were involved.
As far as financial commitments are concerned, perhaps I could name a few. Since 1984, Ottawa has allocated $61 million to the construction of the Biotechnology Research Institute and earmarked the modest sum of $104 million for the manufacture of F-18 aircraft.
Still in the aerospace industry, Pratt and Whitney was granted nearly $152 million. Spar Aerospace enjoyed financial support to the tune of $130 million and Canadair received $50 million.
These figures are certainly not neglible, and they reflect considerable effort and political will on the part of the Government to guarantee the economic survival of a region that is the motor of Quebec's economy and contributes very substantially to the economic development of the entire country. I almost forgot the $200 million that went to General Motors, in addition to the interest-free loan of $110 million for the same company. But since our voluble colleague for Montreal-Sainte-Marie accused us of doing nothing, Mr. Speaker, I would like to remind him of some of our most significant accomplishments in supporting Montreal's own role as a business metropolis. To complement those employment efforts, Canada Employment and Immigration also did its part after CREEM's report was tabled. A special retraining committee was established to help former Montreal East workers retrain.
Finally, I would like to mention the Federal Development Bank's contribution: 480 loans, all in eastern Montreal, for a total of $125 million.
Speaking of banking, the Hon. Member earlier mentioned our position on banking centres. I would simply like to remind him, in order to bring him back to reality, of the Liberal position which was published in the report of the Standing Committee on Finance and Economic Affairs, and I am quoting from the Liberal position:
Supply
"We do not favour the concept of banking centres since they are divisive and ineffectual".

"We do not favour the concept of banking centres since they are divisive and ineffectual."
Therefore, Mr. Speaker, when they suggest we came short of what was needed and that party's position provides for this or that, I ask myself: Well, who speaks on behalf of the Liberal Party of Canada?
If you think that Montreal East alone is facing economic difficulty, I am sorry, and the term is well chosen, I have to set the record straight. We can look at south-western Montreal for instance where the situation has been deteriorating since well before 1984. Such work involves a lot of hard thinking and its results are obviously difficult to discern in the short term. It is not as spectacular as announcing a $50 million subsidy which could extend the life of a company by a year or two. What we are trying to do is something structural and long-lasting which will be more beneficial to the community than the half-baked programs of the former Government.
I am certain that the work of the Southwest Montreal Recovery Comittee, for instance, will lead to results and solutions which will bring this underprivileged region out of its stagnation once and for all.
In its great wisdom, the Opposition has also accused us of being reluctant to implement the recommendations of the Picard Report, also known as the Report of the Advisory Committee on the Development of the Montreal Region. subsubtopic: LANGUAGE TEACHERS-DEMONSTRATION ON PARLIAMENT HILL
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, at noon, some 700 Public Service language teachers will be demonstrating right here on Parliament Hill, to show their frustration with the Conservative Government that leaves its employees without a collective agreement for more than two years. That situation, Mr. Speaker, is absolutely unacceptable. So much so since the Conservative Government proposes to reduce working conditions of Public Service language teachers.
In fact, the Government wants to eliminate the preparation time that is absolutely necessary to all teachers, including Public Service language teachers. Besides, there is a precedent elsewhere, Mr. Speaker, and Public Service language teachers should keep their acquired rights. I am urging the responsible Minister, the President of the Treasury Board (Mr. Mazan-kowski), to go out at noon and to address those militants, those workers, and to undertake to recognize the rights of Public Service language teachers.

subtopic: GREAT LAKES WATER QUALITY AGREEMENT-AMENDMENTS WELCOMED
GREAT LAKES WATER QUALITY AGREEMENT-AMENDMENTS WELCOMED
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, two out of every three Canadians receive their drinking water from the Great Lakes. The Lakes also support economic activity that accounts for one half of the Gross National Product of our entire country. They are, in fact, one of the most important economic and environmental areas in North America.
Because of their importance, Canada and the United States signed the Great Lakes Water Quality Agreement in 1978 to help clean up pollution in the system. Thanks to the efforts of the present Minister of the Environment (Mr. McMillan), amendments to that agreement have been made which will make the clean-up more effective.
Specific targets and goals for decreasing pollution in the Lakes have been set, and both countries will be involved in identifying toxics in the water and developing new techniques to remove them. The agreement will also be more effective in reducing the flow of dangerous pollutants into the water and in implementing new anti-pollution regulations.
The new Great Lakes Water Quality Agreement, together with a new federal water policy, are giving Canadians the



March 18, 1988

assurance they deserve that their environment is clean and safe.

subtopic: DEPORTATION OF CERTAIN REFUGEES-REQUEST THAT MINISTER SUSPEND DEPORTATION ORDER
DEPORTATION OF CERTAIN REFUGEES-REQUEST THAT MINISTER SUSPEND DEPORTATION ORDER
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, a most distressing situation is likely to occur in Montreal on Sunday, when 40 people who entered Canada in good faith and who took advantage of a bad publicity to settle in Montreal... but I do not want to deal with the substance of the issue. But when I see that Kathleen Verdon, a member of the Executive Committee of the City of Montreal, has sent a telegram to the Minister, and that Gerald LeBlanc, from La Presse, one of our most serious journalists, has stated that, unfortunately in its attempt to remedy a bad situation, the Minister of Employment and Immigration (Mr. Bouchard) is about to create one which is even worse. Mr. Speaker, Canada is a country which welcomes immigrants and which-I will readily admit-is faced with a difficult situation because some people entered this country through different means, although now quite well integrated to the Quebec society, the Montreal society, and whose children as we saw yesterday are very well integrated to the French schools and who, together with their young friends with deeper Quebec roots, are already asking: Mr. Speaker, I beg of you, the law exists, it is true, but you are a compassionate man and you should use your powers, the powers you have to end this situation on compassionate grounds and to prevent that, on Sunday, Canada's image be injured.
I therefore ask the Minister of Employment and Immigration (Mr. Bouchard) to use his powers, as his predecessors have always done, to make an exception and to at least postpone the deportation of these people until a proper solution can be found.

subtopic: OPPOSITION TO FOOD IRRADIATION-ABSENCE OF DETECTION TESTS
OPPOSITION TO FOOD IRRADIATION-ABSENCE OF DETECTION TESTS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, as in the United Kingdom, the people of the United States are taking another look at the irradiation of food.
Leading educators, scientists, doctors, church leaders and environmentalists held a national news conference in Washington March 15. I am happy to remark that Canadians, through Food Chain and the Canadian Coalition to Stop Food Irradiation, were co-sponsors. The groups made several demands: stop the irradiation of grains, fruits, vegetables, pork and spices, and halt the pending approval in poultry; make full environmental impact statements before new construction of facilities, and redirect the $5 million from promotion and construction to safety.
I understand that soon to be irradiated Washington State apples could find their way into British Columbia. Since there are no detection tests or labelling requirements, how are Canadians to know if their apples are irradiated? Canadians have a right to know.

subtopic: ROUGE RIVER VALLEY IN SCARBOROUGH-OPPOSITION TO SUBDIVISION DEVELOPMENT

subtopic: ROUGE RIVER VALLEY IN SCARBOROUGH-OPPOSITION TO SUBDIVISION DEVELOPMENT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the last remaining wilderness area in Metropolitan Toronto could be ruined by the Ontario Government. The Rouge River Valley in Scarborough contains over 5,000 acres of natural beauty.
Despite its natural beauty and historical significance, despite the enjoyment thousands of people get from the area, the Government of Ontario is determined to develop the Rouge River into a subdivision.
Scarborough is one of the few cities in North America to combine economic development with environmental conservation successfully. That balance must not be upset.
I am proud to join with Scarborough City Council, the Save the Rouge Valley Organization, and thousands of concerned people all across Scarborough in urging the province not to develop the Rouge River Valley. A federal task force on

March 18, 1988
national parks has made a number of proposals for new park ideas. I urge the Ontario Minister of the Environment to work with the federal Minister and help save the Rouge for future generations of Canadians.

subtopic: BRITISH COLUMBIA SALMON ANGLERS-LIMIT ON CATCHES

speakeroldname: Right Hon. John N. Turner (Leader of the Opposition):
subtopic: BRITISH COLUMBIA SALMON ANGLERS-LIMIT ON CATCHES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, according to the Government's own documents, saltwater sport fishing in British Columbia contributes over $600 million annually to the province's economy. More than 300,000 anglers fish in the tidal basins every year, and over half of those people fish for salmon.
I met earlier this week in Nanaimo with men and women from the South Georgia Strait whose livelihood comes from sport fishing. They are deeply disturbed that the Minister of Fisheries and Oceans (Mr. Siddon) who is, after all, a British Columbia Member of Parliament, cut back the annual limit for salmon for sport fishermen from 20 to 8 without adequate consultation. These British Columbians tell me that they have had difficulty getting the ear of the Minister and that the idea of spot closures without notice is completely unfair to them since they cannot operate their businesses if their businesses can be shut down at any time.
I have more than 100 representations that I will be forwarding to the Minister from people who know the importance of conservation, who know the importance of protecting our fish stocks because they make their living from them and who only expect to be treated in a fair manner, be given a fair hearing, and be able to operate from month to month and from year to year with some certainty.
I urge the Minister to listen to his fellow British Columbians.

CANADIAN RADIO-TELEVISION AND TELECOMMUNICATIONS COMMISSION DECISION REJECTING BELL CANADA RATE APPLICATION APPLAUDED
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise to applaud the Canadian Radio-Television and Telecommunications Commission's decision to deny Bell Canada's so-called rate rebalancing application. I was pleased that NDP Members of Parliament, including my friends from Thunder Bay-Nipigon (Mr. Epp) and Thunder Bay

Atikokan (Mr. March 18, 1988

Angus), with the help of the Hon. Member for Broadview- Greenwood (Ms. McDonald), and myself in Vancouver, were able to appear before the CRTC hearings.
The rejection of a local phone rate increase and the reduction in B.C. Tel and Bell long distance rates is a victory for Canadian consumers, at least for this year. However, I sharply disagree with some of the remarks made in the CRTC decision supporting rate rebalancing in principle. subtopic: PROPOSED TRANSPORTATION OF PLUTONIUM OVER POLAR ROUTE
PROPOSED TRANSPORTATION OF PLUTONIUM OVER POLAR ROUTE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on plutonium overflights there was last week both good and bad
news. First, the good news. We were told that the U.S. will not transport plutonium over Canada. This is even better news for the Minister of Transport (Mr. Crosbie) who managed to waffle his way through this issue without taking a stand on the protection of the health of Canadians. For this, the Minister owes one to Secretary of State Shultz.
Now the bad news. The U.S. Government still intends to transport plutonium from Europe to Japan via a polar route north of Canadian territory. Plutonium released because of an accident could be dispersed over great distances, without respect for political boundaries. Therefore, the population is still at risk. It is thus absolutely essential that the Government of Canada urge Washington to drop the idea of transporting plutonium by air anywhere in the world.
The question now is, will the Minister of Transport take to heart this issue and at last make representations to the U.S. administration on behalf of the world community?

subtopic: NAVY THREATENS TO PULL THE PLUG
NAVY THREATENS TO PULL THE PLUG
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, Nanaimo is known world-wide for having the cleanest politicians around. This is not only because of our outstanding moral fibre. Each July, hundreds of hearty souls climb into leaky "ships of fate" to win the Golden Plug, and each year the Canadian navy provides logistical support.

Mr. Speaker, a report recently made public assesses the status of female RCMP members. That survey of male and female officers in British Columbia concludes that some policies of the police force are instrumental in creating obstacles to women's careers. In addition, the report emphasizes that male members still harbour very negative attitudes toward their female colleagues.

March 18, 1988
Oral Questions

The RCMP Commissioner, however, when asked about this internal report, claimed that the problems women now face in the force are no different from the ones men must confront. This statement ignores the reality of women working in nontraditional occupations and in fact confirms one of the conclusions of the report, which is that traditional social norms and values and deeply ingrained sex-role images which predetermine many attitudes of male members, the public, and the female members themselves, are at the root of the unique difficulties women often experience.

subsubtopic: DISPATCH OF AMERICAN SOLDIERS TO HONDURAS-REQUEST THAT GOVERNMENT INFORM UNITED STATES OF ITS POSITION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my question is for the Deputy Prime Minister. Yesterday President Reagan of the United States sent troops to Honduras. That action was contrary to the Canadian Government's official policy as expressed by the Prime Minister and the Secretary of State for External Affairs.

In Vancouver, for example, the Prime Minister said at a conference of the Inter-American Press Association:
We do not approve of third party intervention anywhere in Central America whoever the third party may be and regardless of its legitimate interest in the area.

Given that policy, did the Canadian Government clearly inform the U.S. Government of its opposition to this intervention in Honduras?

speakeroldname: Hon. Pat Carney (Minister for International Trade):

Whatever the case, there is a clear indication from our sources that there is a major Nicaraguan Government offensive against the Contra resistance. Our concern is that this is happening on the eve of cease-fire discussions which were due to take place on Monday.
Consequently, today we are calling in the American Ambassador and the Nicaraguan Ambassador to say that Canada has grave concerns that the actions which are taking place could undermine the peace effort which has involved so much commitment from so many people.

subsubtopic: CONSTITUTIONAL JURISDICTION-MEECH LAKE ACCORD
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my question is directed to the Minister of Fisheries and Oceans. Premier Peckford stated yesterday in the Newfoundland House of Assembly that a clause in the Meech Lake Accord will lead to greater provincial jurisdiction, specifically Newfoundland and Labrador jurisdiction, over the fishery. The Minister knows that Canada's fish stocks are currently managed by the Government of Canada.
Does the Minister share Premier Peckford's interpretation of the Meech Lake agenda clause on the fishery? Specifically, is he ready to say to the House today that Ottawa is prepared to cede part of its constitutional jurisdiction in the fishery to the Government of Newfoundland and Labrador, or, for that matter, to any other provincial Government?

speakeroldname: Hon. Thomas Siddon (Minister of Fisheries and Oceans):
subsubtopic: CONSTITUTIONAL JURISDICTION-MEECH LAKE ACCORD
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the Hon. Member raises a very important question indeed. The spirit of the Meech Lake Accord is that the respective provincial and federal Governments should be willing to sit down from time to time and talk about matters of mutual interest and concern. In that spirit a clause was inserted in the Accord to the effect that, on a regular basis, First Ministers would review the roles and responsibilities of the federal and provincial Governments regarding the management and allocation of our fish stocks.
It is clearly understood by all provincial Governments that the Constitution of Canada recognizes the responsibility of the federal Government under the Fisheries Act for the management of the fishery. I see nothing wrong with sitting down
March 18, 1988

from time to time, as I do regularly, with my provincial colleagues to talk about the extent to which they offer advice and input on the management process. We have met over a dozen times in the past year and a half, and that kind of dialogue should continue. However, it is not my intention to suggest any ceding of ultimate responsibility by the federal Government for the fishery in this context.

speakeroldname: Mr. Brian Tobin (Humber-Port au Port-St. Barbe):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I thank the Minister for his response. He will know this issue is causing a great deal of consternation and concern in Atlantic Canada and, I suggest, British Columbia as well. On the one hand we have Premier Peckford claiming publicly that the clause will lead to Ottawa ceding jurisdiction over the fishery to provincial Governments, specifically Newfoundland. On the other hand, Premier Buchanan claims the clause is there merely to provide a mechanism for discussion at First Ministers' conferences once a year.
Will the Minister say clearly for the benefit of all Atlantic Canadians and all provinces what the intent is of the clause? Can he say clearly whether or not Premier Peckford's interpretation is correct?

speakeroldname: Hon. Thomas Siddon (Minister of Fisheries and Oceans):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, first, if I read the story in the press this morning, I would read that Mr. Peckford's position is that only Newfoundlanders should be able to fish off their coast. I should point out that is not a quotation of Mr. Peckford or any representative of his Government because that is not his position or that of his Government. For example, fishing vessels from Nova Scotia have for a long time fished on the Grand Banks, as have many foreign vessels which we are now eliminating from that fishery as a matter of government policy.
We are quite content to sit down and discuss these arrangements as reflected in the Meech Lake Accord, but I can tell the Hon. Member that the Newfoundland Minister of Fisheries has at no time indicated to me any suggestion that management responsibility be taken from the federal Government. That is not the objective of the Province of Newfoundland. It is that we continue to discuss jointly and determine what is in the best interests of all Atlantic Canadians in the way in which the fishery is managed.

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, the federal Government does not become directly involved in the adoption process. Mr. Speaker, this question is quite relevant since on July 14, 1978, the present Leader of the Liberal Party stated, and rightly so, that Montreal was a city on the decline and in transition. He added that its national role had diminished. That was right too, although this trend was more obvious in the last four years. He said also that Montreal had lost its financial power, that its service industries were losing ground, its harbour was not longer prosperous and the most active, its manufacturing sector was struggling for survival. Then he said that after years and years of negligence and foreign competition, its airports were no longer the main gateway to the country for international travellers and that its reputation as a congenial city was tarnished. And so on and so on. In conclusion he said that problems in Montreal did not happen overnight and that most of them were its own fault.
Mr. Speaker, I beg to differ with the conclusion of the Leader of the Official Opposition. Montreal is not really responsible for what happened. We never accepted that. The problem is that the former Government did not play its role, although Members from the Hon. Member's Party were well aware of the situation. What action did they take? My hon. colleague for Montreal-Sainte-Marie made three speeches in three years. That is it. And 4,000 jobs were lost.
When we came to power in 1984, we sat down with people at the regional level. We met with all concerned people in the cultural, industrial, artistic community or in the labour movement. We made recommendations and three and a half years later, we have managed to create 114,000 new jobs. We have a booming and striving economy. We now have a base to build on. If I were a Liberal, I would be ashamed today. How dare Liberals claim that Montreal is a victim of its own mistakes, when the city was driven to its ruin by the mistakes of the previous Government. But, the actions of the present Government are rebuilding Montreal, and making it an international capital again.

I believe that if we took an honest look, if we analysed the problem with some measure of reason, there is something we would have to say. We would have to say, as Gerard LeBlanc has said in the press, that one must not, as Jean-Claude Malepart has so often done, link plant shutdowns in the East directly with poverty in that area and that the entire metropolitan area is affected by the industrial crisis in Montreal East. The crisis is visible in my own riding of Essex-Windsor, where there are a lot of closures-and the same can be said of Hamilton, where shutdowns abound, and also of many regions in the province of Quebec, where a great number of plants have closed down and all this is the result of the policy void which exists with regard to industrialization in our country.
It can truly be said, Mr. Speaker, that what we have here, which is similar to what many analysts have encountered in parts of the United States, is a situation of disindustrialization, one where our manufacturing sector is in a lot of trouble. And these problems are not getting the full attention of this Government.
Mr. Speaker, I really believe that the trade agreement with the United States is a step which will result in a worsening of the situation for our industrial sector, throughout the country as well as in Montreal East. I must say, however, Mr. Speaker, although we recognize that this is not only a problem which concerns Montreal East, that there are many things which people who work in Montreal West did, very important things to support this part of the city which is very significant in the history of all countries, the City of Montreal.
If we take the example of Montreal East, we must say first that some figures really give an idea of the size of the problem, such as: about 22,000 unemployed in this part of the city, about 9,400 welfare recipients and close to 7,500 group dismissals over five years. Those figures can be found in a document released by the Comittee for the Economic Renewal of Montreal East. The Committee for the Economic Renewal of Montreal East made important recommendations, and we

give our support to those recommendations, particularly: 1. The Conservatives had promised that this government would bring about changes. This is not the kind of future Canadian men and women wish for their country. This is not what our fellow citizens are demanding. We want something different.
I think if we look at East Montreal and at the problems which have developed there, the tremendous number of shutdowns which have taken place, we can see above all the failure of this Government to put in place an industrial policy which will show some direction in the auto sector, in petrochemicals and in metallurgy, parts of the economy which have traditionally supplied the jobs of eastern Montreal and the southeastern region associated with it.
The Government has not taken that direction. It refuses to provide that leadership. It says instead the answer is somehow to be found lying over the rainbow in a flawed free trade deal with the United States. That kind of approach has simply told the people of East Montreal that this Government is not interested and is not prepared to provide direction, that it is not prepared to lead.

We believe, in our party, that the survival committee put in place for Montreal East is very important. On behalf of our party, the Hon. Member for Ottawa Centre (Mr. Cassidy) gave this committee the widest participation possible, thus indicating that there are true answers to the issues involved, and not only the type of answers that consist of washing one's hands off the problem and saying: "There are already many jobs and we do not need to do anything for that part of the city".
Personally, I do not think it will be possible to carry on with this kind of Government. It is necessary to replace this Government, its policies and to develop an industrial strategy which will address the issue of jobs as well as the industrial vocation of Canada generally and Montreal East in particular. It will not be possible with the trade deal with the United States to give many industries the necessary support to ensure the recovery of Montreal East. It is just not possible!
The Parliamentary Secretary is aware of it, because the Deputy Minister of Finance stated before a committee that we will have to change our regional development policy entirely. It is also impossible for us with the trade deal to do things in the car manufacturing industry to ensure that a company such as Hyundai buy parts here in Canada and creates jobs too.
For these reasons, Mr. Speaker, we certainly support this motion. It is a motion which tells the truth, but not the whole truth, because this Government is faced with many problems, including major ones in Montreal East which it has inherited from past Liberal Governments. As for us, we have to work as hard as possible to establish with the City of Montreal and with Montreal East a most important and profitable industry for our future economy. To do so, I hope the Government will accept this report and all the recommendations made by the Committee for the recovery of Montreal East.

Mr. Speaker, first of all, I would like to congratulate the Hon. Member for Montreal-Sainte-Marie (Mr. Malepart) for taking the initiative to present this motion today, condemning the Conservative Government with respect to the economic situation in Montreal East and the south western region of that city.
Mr. Speaker, usually the resolutions or motions we present in the House concern regions other than the Montreal area. Until today, motions condemning the Government tended to focus on the economic situation in the Gaspe or the Saguenay-Lac Saint-Jean area or, as in the case of the Domtar Plant in early 1985 ...
We have now reached the point where such motions concern regions that would not normally be the focus of this kind of attention on the part of parliamentarians in their concern for regional development.
Mr. Speaker, in the Montreal area the situation has become serious enough to make the Hon. Member for Montreal

Sainte-Marie decide to propose this debate, in order to draw the attention of the Government and to focus public opinion.
We know that Montreal East-and we have been discussing the subject for quite sometime-has 22,000 unemployed and 12,000 people on welfare, and this within a territory covering only five or six ridings.
In the south west region, unemployment is mainly due to plant shutdowns. The list is a familiar one, but I would like to recall the closing of the Gulf Refinery, La Parisette, certain sectors of Bombardier, especially those related to the railways, Vickers, and the list goes on. We are talking about plant shutdowns where men and women who have been employed by these plants for years suddenly found themselves out of a job. This AIDS virus, in the form of plant closures, has spread from Montreal East to the southwest of the city. That was pointed out last Thursday March 17, in La Presse, a Montreal newspaper, that also gave a list of businesses that have shut down: Siemens, 163 jobs lost; Coleco, 730 jobs lost; Sherwin-William, 300 jobs lost; Building Coticelli, 225 jobs lost; Redpath Sugar, 600 jobs lost; and Northern Electric, 60 jobs lost. That list is not complete since there were other closures coupled now with that great concern about a possible closure or possible contract losses at the CN Workshops of Pointe-Saint-Charles.

March 18, 1988

Mr. Speaker, the southwestern part of Montreal is now crying for help because of plant closures and because people with 20 or 25 years of service are faced with unemployment since the skills they acquired after all those years are not easily usable in other industries.
Mr. Speaker, while rumors spread about possible closures in Montreal East, we know that a Damocles sword threatens textile workers in the southwestern part of the city. This is possibly the most serious issue that faces Montreal or, I should say, the whole Canadian garment industry.
Mr. Speaker, the free trade agreement with the United States will have a double-edged sequel: first it will eliminate custom duties, but then companies which produce and market high fashion clothing will find the going even rougher because most of the fabrics they use to make garments-an industry which employs tens of thousands of workers-are imported from abroad, and in most cases these fabrics are not even made in Canada because these are sought-after specialty fabrics used by a fashion-conscious industry. Canadian companies must travel the world over to find them, but under the trade agreement signed with the Americans these imported fabrics will not be allowed on the U.S. market. The point is that the Prime Minister of Canada (Mr. Mulroney), who claims that the free trade agreement with the United States will solve all our economic woes, has endorsed an agreement which does not recognize the country of origin where these products are made and which even excludes any textile product whose basic material is imported from a third country. The ultimate result is that Canadian companies, particularly those which are related to high fashion clothing-most of them in Montreal-will no longer have access to the American market. That is what we will get from the agreement which the Prime Minister of Canada has been boosting as the key to freer trade, the deal with which Canadian firms will open the doors to a market of 250 million consumers.
Among all businesses which will be affected by the free trade deal with the Americans, the clothing industry-it directly employs 110,000 people in Canada, roughly 60,000 in Quebec-will be hardest hit because as an industry it is involved in the so-called free trade agreement, yet in this particular instance it will be denied access to the U.S. market.
To make the situation somewhat less aggravating it has been decided to set a limit in the form of import quotas on these fabrics used to make clothes.
Mr. Speaker, when we talk of liberalizing trade, when we talk of an agreement that will open the U.S. market to Canadian manufacturers and when we limit the sales capacity of those businesses by restricting their ability to buy raw materials, I am wondering what kind of a trade agreement this is. We were right to say from the very beginning that if we do not have any problem with the concept of free-trade, we have considerable difficulties with the type of agreement that was
signed, which is unacceptable for the Montreal region, and particularly for the garment industry.
Mr. Speaker, this Government, this Conservative Party made promises to the Canadian people during the election campaign, particularly to the textile and garment manufacturers who employ so many workers.
Mr. Speaker, during a meeting in Sherbrooke in July of 1984, right in the middle of the campaign-I have here the press releases which were then published by the Conservative Party-they talked, as can be seen on page 2, item 5 of the press relase, of rationalizing Canadian production through the use of mechanisms and remission of duties to allow Canadian manufacturers to deal with foreign manufacturers of inexpensive goods while promoting Canadian expertise in sectors like fashion, marketing, and financing of foreign-made products distributed elsewhere in the world.
Mr. Speaker, the French translation that I just read is not very good and one must read the English version to understand what it is all about since it was probably written in English in the first place. But what does that mean? The Conservative Party made a commitment with the Canadian companies importing quality textile from countries other than the United States. It would grant duty remission to reduce production costs and thus insure greater access and competitiveness on new markets. They were to benefit from Canadian duty remission not only for textile but also for clothes. That was a commitment made by the Conservative Party.
Yesterday or the day before, the Minister of Finance stated in his answers to questions by me and my colleague from Winnipeg-Fort Garry (M. Axworthy): Show us a single statement whereby the Conservative Party or the Conservative Government offered a duty remission like the one the Canadian Apparel Manufacturers Institute is asking for today, arguing that the industry needs help because if the Free Trade Agreement signed with the United States becomes effective, there will be 65,000 jobs lost in Quebec only, of which 25,000 in the Montreal region. We cannot afford to loose 25,000 jobs in an industry employing so many women who acquired skills over the years. Surely, we cannot afford to loose those jobs. People in that industry, in that private sector which is supposed to like the Conservatives, said that they will simply close their plants in Montreal to move to the United States from where, thanks the trade deal, they will be in a position so sell in Canada anyway without having to cope with all sorts of restrictions on their textile imports which are essential to produce top quality clothes.
Mr. Speaker, if we cannot believe employers crying for help to protect Canadian men and women, I wonder exactly where we can find that knowledge of the issues and where we can find the truth.
Mr. Speaker, in a letter dated November 16, 1987, the Minister of Regional Industrial Expansion (Mr. de Cotret) said to the Canadian garment industry, and I quote:
March 18, 1988



"With regard to duty remission programs the Government has long been on record as favouring these for both the apparel and the textile industry".
Mr. Speaker, the Minister of Finance was saying yesterday: Give me a quote. That reminds me of the time Mr. Bourassa asked for evidence in the National Assembly in Quebec. His own colleague, the Minister of Regional Industrial Expansion (Mr. de Cotret), said the Government had committed itself to duty remission. The $200 million a year that are involved will make the apparel industry of Canada able to compete with the Americans. But we now find ourselves in what I would call a Catch-22 situation, where the Government put us. The Americans will reject as unacceptable any duty remission our Government will grant. They will come and dictate policy to the Canadian Government and force it to maintain duties on products coming from third countries. Is that what is called political sovereignty of a country? Imagine having Washington dictate to us, Canadians who have elected our own government, the level of duties we should or could impose on products from abroad!
So, Mr. Speaker, the prospect I raised on previous occasions about the agreement the Prime Minister of Canada signed with his friend Ronald Reagan leading to a customs union sooner or later, and rather sooner than later, is exactly what we see happening in the textile and apparel sector. We are forced, under the threat of possible countervailing duties our apparel industry could be hit with by the Americans, to set our customs duties at the same level as theirs and often higher than theirs are now.
Mr. Speaker, the country of origin rule in the trade agreement normally requires, according to specific industries, between 50, 60 per cent of Canadian content to be granted access to the American market, or 30 per cent in other types; in the case of the textile industry, the percentage is null. And this is why we had to use import quotas on products, raw materials used in garments.
The Minister in charge of the Montreal area should take that situation extremely seriously because 25,000 jobs are at stake, and not only this is 25,000 jobs involving a lot of women, but this is an industry that has been for some years experiencing significant growth, thanks to programs established in the mid-70s. I think they started in 1972-73, when successive Governments in Quebec helped the industry by organizing fashion shows, so that little by little Canadian designers based in Montreal succeeded in getting a degree of international recognition that is some matter of pride for the Canadian garment industry.
Now, because of this trade agreement and the inability or impossibility of the Minister of Finance to respect his own commitments, thousands of jobs will be lost, women will

But let us take the example we have today. The Quebec government, under pressure from the federal Government, which in turn reacts to pressure from the White House, has raised its stumpage duties and has changed its legislation on forestry operations to force logging companies to reforest. And then, everybody goes down to Washington to ask for its blessing, because that is where evrything is settled nowadays.
There was probably a series of discussions with delegates of the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Mr. Masse) or with delegates of the Minister for International Trade who travelled to Washington, where they look at all the figures. How much does it cost to plant a spruce seedling? Nine cents, 14 cents or 15 cents? Washington insists on knowing that, because only then will they be able to decide whether to accept that the federal Government reduces the 15 per cent tax it imposed on our lumber exports.
There are limits, Mr. Speaker. Our political sovereignty in matters of provincial jurisdiction is so jeopardized that, in order to decide what to do with this tax, the Quebec government will have to produce affidavits saying that it costs 14 cents and not 9 cents to plant a small tree, a spruce seedling. The only problem is that several co-ops which started reforestation programs had financial problems because they made too low a bid. And now, Washington starts telling us that according to experiences in the US, it only costs 9 cents!

That is the crux of the matter, Mr. Speaker. I have spoken with people who took part in the discussions, who represent the corporate sector, and that is what they told me. I do not think that they are all liars!
But the truth is, Mr. Speaker, that in key sectors such as this one, this Government has placed Canadian businesses as well as Canadian and provincial jurisdictions under U. S. rule. This is because at one point some were afraid to do the right thing and bring the matter of the 15 per cent tax on lumber before the international GATT tribunal.
Mr. Speaker, the eastern and southwestern parts of Montreal were affected by the attitude of the Federal Government. I listened to the Minister for Industry, Trade and Commerce talk to us about job increases.
Mr. Speaker, I was listening to Le Point on the CBC French language network when a university professor pointed out that the economic recovery had started before the Conservatives came to power and that all this was not the result of initiatives taken by the Government.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would like first to make a comment for the benefit of the Hon. Member who dealt with the free-trade agreement.
When we talk of free-trade, the Liberal Party says that we will lose our sovereignty. I think that Canadians and Quebecers as well as the members of this House are intelligent enough to know that when one asserts that Canada is giving up its sovereignty, one has to be logical. If we give up our sovereignty, it means that we cannot make any decision. The Leader of the Liberal Party travels throughout the country saying that we have given up the political and cultural sovereignty of our country and the irony of it all, Mr. Speaker, is that he adds: "If I am elected, I will tear up that agreement." Surely if we have lost our sovereignty, he could not tear up the agreement. Therefore his argument clearly does not make any sense and is a lot of rubbish.
The Hon. Member has tried to criticize the Free-Trade Agreement while discussing the economic future of Montreal and its impacts on the Quebec economy. As a member of the Quebec legislature he was in a position to get acquainted with the Quebec economy. I would like to put a question to him. I know that the federal Liberal party thinks that providence has conferred upon it every single quality as well as truth and a sacred right. It is difficult for them to sit in the Opposition.
Could the Hon. Member explain how come the Quebec Government, under the guidance of Premier Robert Bourassa, a good Liberal but someone who knows the Quebec economy and its strengths with his caucus and his Cabinet, how come the Quebec Liberal Party led by Mr. Bourassa supports the Free Trade Agreement contrary to the federal Liberal Party's position?
And could he also explain-since he talked a lot about textiles-the position of Jean-Guy Dionne or Eric Barry from the Canadian Textile Institute? Mr. Dionne has companies in the Beauce area and in Drummondville. Those people know the industry and support the Free Trade Agreement.
Is the federal Liberal Party saying to the Quebec Government: "Bourassa, you and Dionne are both wrong"?

subsubtopic: ALLOTED DAY, S. O. 82-ECONOMIC FUTURE OF REGION OF GREATER MONTREAL
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I appreciate the Minister's question because it will give me the opportunity to raise two others aspects that I had not touched upon in my speech.
Mr. Speaker, in the case of the Free Trade Agreement, Mr. Bourassa has laid down conditions which have not yet been satisfied for him to give his final agreement to free trade.
March 18, 1988

One of the first conditions laid down by Mr. Bourassa, and my colleague will remember the press releases of the Quebec Government, is that the American bill, the Omnibus Trade Bill as it is called, do exempt Canada from its protectionist measures.
Mr. Speaker, it is when the bill finally becomes law, after being passed by the U. S. House of Representatives and Senate, that we will know whether this condition will actually be met.
The second condition has to do with major retraining programs for the workers who will be affected by the trade agreement. Mr. Speaker, the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson) has already told the House that his government and his Department would not propose any special programs or additional funds to assist in the retraining of workers.
Therefore, about that aspect you mentioned, I recognize that, from the point of view of a province that wishes to export electricity, this might prove a positive thing. I do understand the arguments of the Hon. Member who is trying to show that I am contradicting the provincial government. One thing is certain Mr. Speaker, Mr. Bourassa is entitled to his opinion. 1 do recognize it. I have also accepted his conditions for Quebec's final acceptance of this agreement and we will see whether these conditions will actually be met by the friends of the Minister who just asked me the question. As far as 1 am concerned, I think the U.S. Government will never accept to make an exception for Canada in its Omnibus Trade Bill.
As for textiles, Mr. Speaker, this is a completely different matter, and the Hon. Minister's question makes me laugh, because it is not the Liberal party which proposed during its electoral campaign to offer a remission of customs duties paid not only by Canadian textile companies but also by Canadian clothing companies. We did not make that proposal. It is the present Prime Minister, the leader of the Progressive Conservative party, who promised a remission of customs duties during his campaign. That promise, Mr. Speaker, has been reiterated by the Minister of Regional Industrial Expansion (Mr. de Cotret) in a letter sent to the Canadian Apparel Manufacturers Institute to tell them that customs duties would be remitted.
Mr. Speaker, it is the Tory Government, the Progressive Conservative party that are in hot water. The Minister can ask me about Mr. Dionne or about the textile industry, that's all right. But I will reply: What is your answer to garment manufacturers? What is your answer as a Cabinet Minister to the allegations made by the industry representatives? Fifteen of them came to see us yesterday or the day before, and they told us about a potention loss of 65,000 jobs in Canada, including 25,000 in Quebec. You can refer to Mr. Dionne or some other people, but what do you answer to Mr. Dionne when you say, for example, that you will offer a remission of all the customs duties and when he asks whether it is for textile or clothing? You are stuck with your promise. It is this Government which promised the garment industry for a $200
Supply
million remission in customs duties. We on this side of the House did not make such a promise.
Then, if you have answers to give to Mr. Dionne, if you have answers to give to the garment industry, you could ask the question to your Prime Minister, to your Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson), to your Minister of Industry and Trade, the Minister of Regional Industrial Expansion (Mr. de Cotret) because they made commitments and they run the risk of closing garment factories in Canada, by not living up to them. I could also talk about furniture manufacturing, as we talk about free trade.
Mr. Speaker, some people come and tell us that they are for free trade, for a Trade Agreement, because now they understand better that you cannot call that free trade.
We, in the Quebec caucus, had the visit of members of the Conseil du Patronat. They came to say that they are for the Trade Agreement, with some reservations. Big deal, Mr. Speaker! If I sit and you get up and ask that those who are in favour of the Bill please rise, when I am sitting, Mr. Speaker, I have a choice. I remain seated or I rise. I do not want to rise halfway up, because you will not count my vote. So this is what it is like when you are for something with reservations; I cannot understand such a position.
Once the general statement delivered, that question was put to every furniture industry representative, mostly household, and not business, and what was the answer of the household furniture industry representative? That he would close the plant to move to Virginia. So I asked him: "Why move to Virginia"? He said that it was simply because "In Virginia, I get the building free for five years and they meet 50 p. 100 of my payroll for the first year, and they also lend me the money at prime less three". He also added: "If I go to Virginia, with the free trade deal, it will cost me $6.50 an hour for labour, and with the exchange rate right now, here, it is costing me $10.50. Since Canada is going to remove its tariffs because of the Prime Minister's Free Trade Agreement, I will be able to supply the Canadian market with the furniture I make down in the states". Then I asked him: "What will happen to your workers, then?" He said: "Well, it is either moving or going bankrupt because I would no longer be able to stand competition." That is the kind of help or the kind of agreement that is supposed to create jobs, jobs and jobs all over the country.
Mr. Speaker, since this debate began, I must confess that I was quite concerned about the agreement. But the more I look at it and discuss it with people from various sectors, the more 1 am convinced that my leader did the right thing.

Mr. Speaker, I have listened to two Liberal Members today with great interest. We have heard today what they are against, not what they are for. Both stood up and both ran off a string of what they perceive to be problems, but they offered no solutions. The Hon. Member who just spoke is a

former provincial cabinet Minister, He did not speak the way he is speaking today when he was in the provincial Government.
I want to cover a couple of items about which he spoke. First, the tax on softwood lumber. The agreement was reached between the provinces and the federal Government on how to best approach this problem. There was a choice. Either the 15 per cent tax would be imposed in the United States and the Americans would collect it to pay off their deficit from our provincial resources or the provinces would receive the money for their coffers.
The Hon. Member is complaining about the tax. That tax money is going back to the provincial Government to be used in the many ways the province can use it. Five provinces have now settled the adjustment procedure on that particular tax. We are close to an agreement with the Province of Quebec.
The Hon. Member fails to mention that we solved the problem of U.S. logs coming into Canada and being processed by Quebec mills which no longer have a source of timber close to them. To keep them alive, they import logs from the United States, dress them here and send the finished lumber back. We have made arrangements that the tax is not on that lumber. He has failed to mention all these things.
The Hon. Member then talked about the furniture dealer who will move to the United States because of the free trade agreement. He failed to ask this fellow about the benefits his workers receive from the Canadian and provincial Governments and whether they will receive those in the United States. When he goes to the United States, he will find that he has to start paying the full cost for a health plan for the workers and he will have to pay the full cost of pension plans. He will have to look at the productivity he gets from those people as compared to the workers in Canada. He will then find that he has a hell of a good deal here in Canada. That same furniture dealer will be able to penetrate a much bigger market in the United States with those tariffs gone. That is the challenge for him, and I believe that he can accept that challenge.
I would be willing to wager that I travel around the country on the free trade agreement a lot more than the Hon. Member does. I find that the more people understand what the free trade agreement says, the more acceptance there is.

It is the same thing in the province of Quebec.

And they will come back and raise them somewhat, and then they will ask the
March 18, 1988

we would really like to address this afternoon is an economic question.
I guess some of the concerns we have are in terms of the economy, particularly. I think it is interesting that the opposition motion should be brought forward at this time because it is symbolic that we are celebrating the anniversary of what has been known as the Shamrock Summit in Quebec City. To the dismay of many Irish people in this country, St. Patrick's Day is not just the celebration of Ireland and St. Patrick any longer but the planting of the seeds of an agreement that is really going to undermine our country in the future. When we look at the economic policies of the Government, and watch what has happened, the erosion that has taken place, and when we talk about the industrial complex in Canada, we are concerned. It concerns me somewhat when we look at our cities and we see the bankruptcy of ideas and vision of the Government when it does not see the ability to put an economic strategy in place in order to have all our cities healthy. It is important that we look at what has caused some of these decisions. Many of the causes have been the result of government policy.
We have a Government that looks only at what the markets will be and at what the bottom line will be. It is using workers, people and communities as commodities that can be moved around. This is not the kind of vision that we have for the country or for the cities of our country.
When I talk of Hamilton today, I talk of Hamilton from the point of view of what has happened to workers in that community. I talk of Montreal East and the Montreal region when I visit my relatives and friends. It is the city of my birth. I understand the great transition that has gone on in Montreal and the terrible things that have happened to it. They have happened because this is an industrialized sector of our economy. This is true whether we talk of Vancouver, Halifax, Montreal, Quebec City, Toronto or Hamilton. This is an industrialized sector of our economy that is being totally eroded. We are entering a trade agreement that guarantees there will be more erosion. This is of great concern to all Canadians.
When we look at this we must recognize what has happened in Quebec. I was interested to hear the comments of the Hon. Member who spoke before me when he referred to the paper industry. I am old enough to remember when the dollar was a dollar and the pulp and paper industry was in very deep trouble. I remember when the American markets became very delicate. We know that there is now research going on in the
