pulp and paper industry that will make it possible for the deep south to be able to manufacture a lot of its paper if the market is such and as our dollar is going up. The present Government refuses to lower the interest rates. We know that another Canadian market is in jeopardy.
When we talk about the trade agreement that is supposed to be so good for the East End of Montreal and for the manufacturing parts of our country, what we really need to talk about is what are the implications of the trade agreement. The implications of the trade agreement seem to get lost when the Government debates that subject. The Government attempts to defend it by saying that we will have access to the American market. It goes both ways. We have very little access to that market and there are heavy transportation costs involved. The Americans wish to be treated by national standards in our financial institutions. speakerposition: Chief Government Whip's assistant; Deputy Whip of the Progressive Conservative Party
subsubtopic: ALLOTED DAY, S. O. 82-ECONOMIC FUTURE OF REGION OF GREATER MONTREAL
speechtext: Twenty years!

subsubtopic: ALLOTED DAY, S. O. 82-ECONOMIC FUTURE OF REGION OF GREATER MONTREAL
speechtext:
We have been going through a major crisis in the last ten years. In my opinion, both the Liberal Government and the Conservative Government are to blame for this situation.
Indeed, the energy policy of Trudeau Government is largely to blame for the disappearance of our petrochemical industry. The Liberal Members were silent at that time, including the Hon. Member for Montreal-Sainte-Marie (Mr. Malepart).
In 1984, the Conservatives took over and disaster struck, beginning with the disappearance of the Gulf refinery. In Montreal East, there are now 22,000 unemployed and 9,400 welfare recipients, and there have been 7,500 lay-offs in five years. Many committees were created. The Prime Minister appointed a Minister responsible for Montreal. The province, the city of Montreal, the employers and the unions all worked together to find solutions to the employment problem. The city of Montreal delivered by contributing $90 million, and so did the province of Quebec by promising $106 million, but, disappointingly, the federal Government only allocated $35 million dollars in new money. However, the Government is generous in its hesitations. For instance, the Government promised a space agency in the throne speech. On February 23, the Minister responsible said that the agency would be set up in 1988. On March 10, Mr. de Cotret stated that there would be no agency. On March 16, the Prime Minister announced in Baie-Comeau that there would indeed be one.
I gave this example in order to illustrate the lack of courage of the Government and its inability to make decisions. The same thing happens practically with every issue: banking centres, railways, etc.
The 31,400 unemployed in Montreal East are waiting for some action from the Government, and not for more pussyfooting. Montrealers want the prosperity back in their area and they do not want to be mesmerized by election promises. This indecisiveness on the part of the Government is bad for private investments. The Government has to make decisions, announce them and carry them out. The Prime Minister said that the development of Montreal is a priority. We ask him today, on behalf of the 31,400 unemployed, to prove it by making the necessary decisions.
It is not difficult to understand how depressed the unemployed are.

It is the type of thing that takes the spirit of a community. It says to people: "You really do not count. I will talk to my friends. I will make my deals with the business community but I am not going to worry about what is happening. I will make speeches so that they will elect me, but I really do not have any sense of commitment to say that these people count and are valuable".
This type of thing is happening right across the country. Millions of dollars are being spent on a sales pitch to say that we are getting into a good trade agreement with the United States. When we have set up panels and have asked for government Members to participate, they refuse to show up. During International Women's Week we had such a panel. We could not get one Conservative Member to appear on the panel. I say "we" collectively as Canadians. I am not speaking as a politician now, I am speaking as a member of the community of Canada.
The Government is allowing one of the greatest cities in the country to be undermined because it has no economic strategy. When we consider the type of programs that have gone on as well as the recommendations of a certain committee's report, we see that the recommendations are strong and valid. The recommendations in the report were formed as a result of listening to a cross-section of the community of Montreal East. When we look at those recommendations, we see that they are a valid strategy for economic development. They look at the skills that are in that community, and at how the future of that community can develop. They take the resources that are there and can be implemented. But there has to be some government help and commitment.
One sees the type of commitment that has been given by the City of Montreal. Certainly the Mayor of Montreal has made it a priority. He recognized the high level of unemployment and how important it is to get those people to work. He asked for readjustment programs for older workers which the Government kept saying that it was going to do, but it has refused to do. When one looks at the commitment given by the Government of Quebec and then one sees a measly $35 million from the federal Government for an area that is in dire need, it
March 18, 1988

is a disgrace. When people say that they have a commitment to the future of this country, we certainly have to look at the consequences of their policies.
When one hears Mr. Parizeau and other people talk about how good the free trade agreement is for the Province of Quebec, it is very important for those of us who feel strongly about having a country that is total to recognize the great danger of that trade agreement the Province of Quebec, as far as tying its economy into the American economy and ignoring the western part of Canada. It is important that we look at the long term effects.
I am not sure the present Government has the capacity of being able to look at the long term. It always seems to be looking at short term ad hoc decisions. For example, today there is a space agency, tomorrow there is not; the next day perhaps we do, but we are not quite sure where we are going to have it. If we take those things seriously and look at the long term for the building of this nation, and building it with a strong economy, we must look at what is happening in the east end of Montreal and recognize that the erosion taking place there will be even greater if there is not some built-in infrastructure to protect that economy now. It is very serious.
I know there has been a lot of hilarity in the Chamber this afternoon. If we were one of the 31,000 who are unemployed, we would not be laughing quite as hard and making such fun and jokes at each other. It is very serious. This part of the city had good manufacturing, textile workers, refineries, and massive employment. Now there is a whole readjustment that has to take place.
If this is the manner in which this Government is addressing readjustment, then goodness help us all when we get into a program with 500,000 jobs going down the drain. We have to look seriously at what is happening. This is a good motion to have before us. It a microcosm of what we will be looking at across the country in the future. If we are not willing to put adjustment programs in place, if we are not willing to look at the communities and what the grass roots skills are, and what their development is, then we will not be willing to look at any future economic strategy.
One can talk about getting "this in my riding, or this in the next riding", but I hope that some day we will get a New Democratic Government that understands what economic strategy and planning is to put some priorities on where people can work; to put some priorities on what is possible for people to have dignity and equality of life; to recognize the heritage and the legacy that we have in the City of Montreal, where the east end of that city is going down the drain and the Government is blinking its eyes and saying that it is not sure and it is changing its mind every day.
It seems to me that we must look at an economic strategy, and listen to committees which have made some very sensible recommendations, which have come from the grass roots, whereby people would have the ownership of their own future. If the Government were willing to implement some of those
Supply
recommendations, we would all live better, be healthier, and see the east end of Montreal come back with the old vitality that it had in days of yore.

Mr. Speaker, how can we possibly give an overview of such an important question in just a few minutes. First of all, I want to repeat what I have always maintained: it is as a result of the great social conscience of our colleague from Montreal-Sainte-Marie (Mr. Malepart) that we could have this debate today. I remember meeting him when he became a Member of Parliament here in Ottawa, although I knew him before. But as of 1979, with the whole team of the Members from Montreal East, in the company and under the leaderchip of Monique Begin, to whom 1 want to pay special homage here, meetings were held every week, I tell you, Mr. Speaker, to discuss the economy of Montreal East, and this for many years. They even signed letters to the Prime Minister of Canada, and I can assure you it is very unusual for ministers to sign a letter asking for certain things to be done, although we all know the problems we were facing at the time.
So I think the Hon. Member for Montreal-Sainte-Marie does not have to be told by anyone in this House what to do, not by our new-found saviours in the New Democratic Party and not by those who want to attack us. I know and can testify to his record and his concerns.
What troubles me as a Montrealer is a short sentence in an outstanding article by Miville Tremblay, where he says, and I am sorry, but this is the quote: "We certainly no longer expect anything from the federal Government". Another quote: "The Conservatives have not only given up on Montreal East but on the entire city ''.That was a quote from Mr. Picard.
I would like to ask the House to think about this statement, because under Mr. Trudeau's Government, we had Members who were the envy of practically the entire caucus. No one can deny the determination of a Marc Lalonde, a Monique Begin, a Gerard Pelletier, a Serge Joyal and an Andre Ouellet, and I
Supply
refer to their determination to take care of the needs of Montreal. This was going on every week at the meetings of the Quebec Caucus. I was there regularly since I was chairman of the caucus, and I know it was one of our major concerns.
What saddens me is that Members of the House do not understand that there are differences in Canada. Jean Marchand, one of the most dynamic Quebecers, and nobody can deny that, sat in this House and always said that Montreal was the economic heart of the Province of Quebec. It is so different from the other provinces! But in Quebec we know very well that when Montreal is in the doldrums the whole province experiences difficulties.
So that is the purpose of the motion introduced by my colleague from Montreal-Sainte-Marie, this is how we try to draw the Government's attention to make decisions.
I know that the world of politics is not for the weak-hearted. There is always some rivalry among the various regions. Only the NDP Members cannot understand that. They are centralizers. With them, everything has to come from Ottawa. This is why their Party will never respond to the aspirations of Quebecers here in Ottawa, because it is a centralizing Party.
Mr. Speaker, I submit that the situation is getting serious, and I suggest the Hon. Member for Levis (Mr. Fontaine) ought to listen to what I am saying. I am saying that the situation is getting serious when Quebec, the Province of Quebec, the Government of Quebec has to hire a lobbyist to get its fair share of federal contracts. One thing I can tell you is that we did have difficulties during the 1980-84 period, and the economic situation was not all that promising. Yet, in spite of that we never had as many complaints as we have now from people in Montreal. We never did get as many complaints as we are now receiving from people in Montreal East. However, Mr. Speaker, when a provincial government is hiring lobbyists as the Quebec government is doing because it cannot find anyone to uphold the vital interests of Montreal, the problem is indeed very serious.
I would have liked to speak at length of this issue, because I made lengthy preparations and I take my work seriously... However, my colleagues from Montreal-Sainte-Marie, and Laval-des-Rapides discussed that issue extensively. I merely wanted to add that the situation is urgent and that we have to understand what Montreal represents for Quebec. Conditions are not similar in other provinces.
So, I thank you, but we will certainly have more to say on the subject later on, Mr. Speaker. In closing, I would like to mention that some people have spent hundreds of thousands of dollars, including friends of the Government, Mr. Peladeau, everybody's friend, a good friend of mine, who went as far as staging a publicity campaign that cost hundreds of thousands of dollars to make the single point about the spatial character of Montreal with the slogan "Montreal, c'est spatial". When will that be understood? Montreal is a space industry center as other regions are automobile industry centers. The space
